clue.text: Setter accepts a second opportunity: it opens out

indicators.note: one word taking in others, as a host accepts guests, so the setter word goes round

parts.note: cement is something that sets hard, so it is a setter
a window is a period of opportunity, as in 'window of opportunity'

explanation.surface: A crossword setter grabs a second chance, and something opens up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' looks like the crossword compiler but is the stuff that sets hard; 'accepts' puts A and S inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of hinged window swings outward from the frame, so it is a thing that opens out.

clue.text: See 10
Wicketkeeper quietly dropped for silly mistake

indicators.note: dropped means a letter is let fall from the word

parts.note: a stumper is an informal name for the wicketkeeper in cricket, who stumps batsmen
P (piano) is the musical abbreviation for quietly

explanation.surface: A cricket keeper is quietly left out of the side after a foolish error.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the wicketkeeper stands behind the stumps; 'dropped' sounds like team selection but removes P.
explanation.definitionFit: A stumer is informal British slang for a dud or blunder, originally a worthless cheque.

clue.text: Virtually — gold?

definitions.meaning: the question invites completing the saying '... gold', so these words stand before gold in it

explanation.definitionFit: Something nearly so is practically the same as being it, hence virtually; the familiar simile completes with gold.

clue.text: Fight to keep the NHS so?

definitions.meaning: a brawl in which everyone joins in
the NHS (Britain's National Health Service) is meant to stay costless to every patient

explanation.surface: A campaign to protect Britain's health service.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl open to anyone is a general melee, and the founding principle of the NHS is care at no charge to anybody.

clue.text: Old-fashioned bum paper

parts.note: bum is British slang for the backside, as is behind
The Times is a British national newspaper

explanation.surface: A dated, rather rude term for toilet paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum paper' reads as toilet roll; it splits into the backside and a newspaper, The Times of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of step with current ways is an idiom for dated or outmoded.

clue.text: No one in particular risking being run over?

definitions.meaning: an ordinary member of the public, the average person
literally, a person standing in the road among the traffic

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the idiom for the typical citizen, and read literally describes a pedestrian out in the roadway.

clue.text: I want more from officer before coming round

indicators.note: the word for before comes round, enclosing the officer

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
NCO is a non-commissioned officer

explanation.surface: An officer heads a request for more before going on rounds.
explanation.definitionFit: An audience shouts this French word to demand a further performance, so it says I want more.

clue.text: See 7
Be editor of Independent, admitting wife is no friend of cyclists

indicators.note: admitting means letting something in, so the wife goes inside

parts.note: to head a newspaper is to be its editor

explanation.surface: Edit The Independent newspaper while the wife rails against cyclists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitting' slips the wife between the two parts of the charade, not inside either one.
explanation.definitionFit: Air blowing against a rider slows progress, so it is the bane of anyone on a bicycle.

clue.text: Small car to tour one's island, or islands

indicators.note: touring means going all round, so the car goes round the other letters

parts.note: the Nissan Micra is a small car
taken as ONES, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Taking a little car round your own island, or islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to tour' wraps the car round the rest; 'island, or islands' makes the plural the definition, with 'or' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This Pacific region is a large group of small islands, so the name stands for islands.

clue.text: Be hard to swallow, as snack in pub: conviction follows

indicators.note: follows means the conviction comes after the first part
in places the snack inside the pub

parts.note: a bar is a pub
an egg is a pub snack, as in a pickled egg
a conviction is a firm belief

explanation.surface: A pub snack that won't go down, followed by a court conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be hard to swallow' and 'snack' suggest food, but the definition means be incredible; 'in' sets the snack inside the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: To be hard to swallow figuratively is to be scarcely credible, the sense of this idiom.

clue.text: Saviours of the planet like Kermit to have fun

parts.note: Kermit the Frog is green
to party is to have fun

explanation.surface: Environmentalists who are, like Kermit, out to enjoy themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: This political group campaigns on environmental issues, casting itself as protectors of the Earth.

clue.text: They're the world's biggest: word does get round

indicators.note: getting round suggests letters turned about and rearranged

explanation.surface: Word spreads about the world's biggest things.
explanation.definitionFit: These Californian sequoias are the tallest trees on Earth, so they are the world's biggest.

clue.text: Remarkable Edith Evans in the lead gets awarded part that can't be changed

indicators.note: remarkable here means re-markable, open to being written out anew
in the lead means the front letter of the name

parts.note: an actor who gets awarded a part is cast

explanation.surface: The actress Edith Evans lands a starring role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkable' rearranges EDITH plus E into THEDIE. Dame Edith Evans was a celebrated British actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's phrase at the Rubicon declares a step irrevocable, so it describes something final and unalterable.

clue.text: Thought: I don't run the paper on whisky!

definitions.meaning: thought here is the past tense of think, as in pictured in the mind

definitions.text: I don't run the paper on whisky!
definitions.meaning: I am the editor of the gin paper, not the whisky one

explanation.surface: An editor protests indignantly that their paper isn't about whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Pictured in the mind or fancied is the sense of thought as a past tense verb.

clue.text: See 15
See 6
Heartily destroy every memory

indicators.note: only the heart of the word is used, its outer letters lost

parts.note: to wreck is to destroy
all means every

explanation.surface: A wholehearted urge to wipe out every recollection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartily' looks like an adverb of enthusiasm but keeps only the middle of WRECK, giving REC.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means the power of remembering, as in total recall, a synonym of memory.

clue.text: Russian notes endless desire to take litre in hard liquor

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the liquor

parts.note: sake is Japanese rice liquor

indicators.note: to take means the shortened word takes the litre after it
endless means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: want means desire

explanation.surface: A Russian scribbles notes about craving vodka by the litre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' drops the last letter of the desire word; 'in' sets that plus L inside the Japanese rice liquor.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's ballet score is a Russian composer's music, so it is a set of Russian notes.

clue.text: See 1
See 12
Sound of bouncing around tail of the plane

indicators.note: around means the sound goes round the letter

parts.note: boing is the sound of something bouncing

indicators.note: tail of means the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bouncing noise from the tail of an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail of the' gives E, placed by 'around' inside BOING.
explanation.definitionFit: The US maker's name is used for its airliners, as in a jumbo jet, so it means an aircraft.

clue.text: Discredit popular girl I go out with

parts.note: in means popular, fashionable
Val is a girl's name
to date is to go out with someone

explanation.surface: A boast: the popular girl is the one I'm going out with.
explanation.definitionFit: To undermine an argument or claim is to show it unsound, rendering it void.

clue.text: See 24 down
Exploit soundly-built farm girl

parts.note: to milk is to exploit

indicators.note: soundly means the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: made means built

explanation.surface: Taking advantage of a sturdy country lass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly-built' looks like sturdy, but 'soundly' asks for a word that sounds like 'made'.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who milks cows on a farm was traditionally a dairy worker, a rural lass.

clue.text: The situation: what a lot of whoppers our country tells!

definitions.meaning: the state of affairs, as in finding out where things stand

definitions.text: what a lot of whoppers our country tells!
definitions.meaning: whoppers are lies, so this exclaims at the way our nation lies

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means the lie of the land, how matters stand; read literally it marvels at the nation's lying.

clue.text: See 25
